They're both retirement savings accounts. Companies generally provide a 401k to employees and match a certain percentage of what the employee puts in. The money that gets put in is pre-tax, therefore providing less taxable income which is generally a good thing - grubby government can take it. The downside is that you're required to wait until you're 65 (the age limit is different in some cases) before you can withdraw the money. If you take any out early, you're taxed at the current tax rate (which will probably be higher) as well as paying penalties for withdrawing. Therefore, your money is locked for decades. Additionally you have no control over what investments are backing your 401k, the fund provider does that.

A Roth IRA on the other hand is usually aquired by a person themselves. The contribution limit is lower than a 401k but you can have more control over how the money is invested.

Ideally, a person should have both.

The purpose of them is to save money, invest it, grow it, and have money when you retire.

A 401(k) is an individual retirement plan run by your employer (almost always farmed out to some sort of investment firm). You voluntarily contribute a percentage of your gross (pre-tax) pay and usually buy some sort of mutual fund or something. The choices tend to be limited and grouped into a projected retirement date window. Your employer typically matches your contribution up to some pitifully small percentage as a benefit. All withdrawals when you retire are then taxed at whatever tax bracket you're in at the time.

An IRA is an individual retirement account. You (or a financial advisor of your choice) control where you retirement contributions go, not your employer or their contracted investment firm. Again, it's pre-tax money, so depending on your financial situation, you can have a lower potential tax bill. You can invest in anything you like, stocks, bonds, mutual funds, real estate, precious metals, whatever the hell you want. Again, all withdrawals are taxed when you take them.

These both have Roth counterparts where instead of pre-tax money, you use net income (the pre-tax contributions are called Traditional as opposed to Roth). It's already been taxed, so when you retire and withdraw, you don't have to pay federal taxes on it (for now, who knows what the greedy cockbags will do in the future).

You can have both a 401(k) and an IRA, and you can have Traditional and Roth accounts for each. There are contribution limits, but if you're still young, odds are you won't hit those limits any time soon.

Any investment is potentially risky, but putting money in a safe effectively guarantees it will lose value due to inflation. 401(k) is a tax-deferment retirement setup. You take a part of your paycheck, and you place it in this retirement account before it is taxed. These are employer sponsored, and take the place of a true "pension" system. Employers often cover the cost of the program, and some will match a percentage of the money you place in the account. The money is always yours, unlike a pension, and you can take it with you when you leave that company. (There are "vesting" rules for most, where you only get to keep the "employer" portions base don how long you work there.)
The idea is that you will put aside this money, pre-tax, and then, when you are retired, you start pulling it out, and are taxed on it then. The good part is, any increase in value of the account due to investment gain is not taxed. You get taxed only when you remove money form the account. The bet you are making is that the tax rate during your retirement will be less than it is throughout your lifetime. Since your income will be SS (if it exists then) and your 401(k) outflows, your tax rate is going to be small compared to the majority of your career, so instead of being in the 25% marginal tax bracket like when you worked, you might only be in the 15% tax bracket as a retired fella. IRAs - Individual Retirement Accounts. These can be pre-tax, post-tax, or a combination. There are two main types, Traditional and Roth.

Roth IRAs are funded post-tax, BUT are tax-free upon disbursement, with some rules. Any gains the account made, you will pay taxes on once your contribution value has been met if they occur before you are 60 or before the funds have been there for 5 years. Example - you put in $100k over your working career into a Roth IRA. At retirement, the account i worth $500k. The first $100k you withdraw is tax free no matter what. If you are 60 AND the $400k in gains have been there for 5 years or more, you can continue pulling out cash tax free.

Traditional IRAs work similar to a 401(k), where you are allowed to defer taxes on money deposited, and you get taxed upon withdrawal. The difference is that he plans are not employer sponsored, so they are yours, which means investment options are less restricted, but you will have to pay the cost of the account maintenance, trading fees, etc. and there is no additional funding from your employer.
